subject: paediatrics
title: Neonatal Sepsis, Diagnostic Screen and Blood Culture

steps.tx: Systemic bacterial infection manifesting within the initial seventy-two hours of life defines **early onset neonatal sepsis**. Acquired vertically from the maternal genital tract through ascending amniotic infection or during passage through the birth canal, it typically presents fulminantly with acute respiratory distress, severe hypothermia, poor peripheral perfusion, and rapidly progressive septic shock.
steps.say: Early-onset sepsis manifests within seventy-two hours from maternal vertical transmission.

rows: Meningitis, focal bone or joint infections

steps.tx: The primary perinatal risk factors predisposing to early infection include maternal chorioamnionitis, maternal intrapartum fever exceeding thirty-eight degrees Celsius, and **prolonged rupture of membranes**. Amniotic membrane rupture exceeding eighteen hours permits rapid ascending bacterial colonization of fetal respiratory membranes, multiplying the risk of invasive early-onset sepsis.
steps.say: Membrane rupture beyond eighteen hours significantly increases the risk of ascending neonatal sepsis.

left.title: Major Perinatal Risk Factors
points: Membrane rupture exceeding 18 hours
Maternal chorioamnionitis or foul liquor
Maternal intrapartum pyrexia over 38 degrees C

right.title: Neonatal Susceptibility Factors
points: Prematurity under 37 weeks gestation
Low birth weight under 2500 grams
Low 5-minute Apgar score under 6

steps.tx: Objective laboratory evaluation utilizes a standardized multi-parameter **neonatal sepsis screen panel**. A positive screen requires two or more abnormal parameters among total leukocyte count, absolute neutrophil count, immature to total neutrophil ratio, micro-erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, providing ninety percent negative predictive value.
steps.say: The sepsis screen requires two abnormal parameters to guide empirical antibiotic decisions.

rows: Most sensitive early indicator of neutrophil left shift
Neutropenia has higher specificity than neutrophilia
Over 15 mm in the first hour
Rises 12 to 24 hours after inflammatory onset

steps.tx: A rapid bedside hematological index is the **micro erythrocyte sedimentation rate**, performed using non-heparinized capillary tubes filled with anticoagulated blood. Tubes are stood vertically for sixty minutes. An erythrocyte fall exceeding fifteen millimeters in the first hour indicates systemic inflammation, matching standard Westergren performance with minimal blood volume requirements.
steps.say: Micro-ESR provides rapid bedside assessment of inflammation using capillary blood in an hour.

left.title: Micro-ESR Technique
points: Heparinized capillary tube filled to 50 mm
Stood vertically for exactly 60 minutes
Erythrocyte meniscus fall measured in millimeters

right.title: Clinical Interpretation
points: Normal: age in days plus 3 mm (under 15 mm)
Abnormal: fall greater than 15 mm in first hour
Not influenced by gestational age or birth weight

steps.tx: Synthesized by hepatocytes in response to interleukin-six, the acute-phase reactant **serum C-reactive protein** provides invaluable longitudinal guidance. Because hepatic CRP synthesis requires twelve to twenty-four hours to peak, initial levels may be normal in early infection. However, two consecutive normal CRP measurements taken twenty-four hours apart demonstrate high negative predictive value.
steps.say: Serial normal CRP levels twenty-four hours apart safely exclude sepsis and allow stopping antibiotics.

rows: Initiate empirical antibiotics if clinical sepsis suspected
Rises to peak if infection true
Elevated CRP confirms active inflammatory state
Safely discontinue antibiotics if cultures are sterile

steps.tx: The absolute diagnostic gold standard for confirming neonatal bacteremia is a **sterile peripheral blood culture**. A minimum blood volume of one milliliter must be inoculated into a pediatric automated culture bottle prior to administering antimicrobial therapy. Drawing blood from umbilical arterial catheters is avoided due to the hazard of line colonization artifacts.
steps.say: One milliliter of blood drawn sterilely before antibiotics constitutes the gold standard culture.

left.title: Blood Culture Technique
points: Clean skin with 70% alcohol and chlorhexidine
Draw at least 1.0 mL blood from peripheral vein
Inoculate automated pediatric blood culture bottle

right.title: Technical Pitfalls
points: Volumes under 0.5 mL yield false negatives
Catheter draws frequently contaminated
Antibiotic pretreatment suppresses bacterial growth

steps.tx: Because clinical signs of meningitis are subtle and open cranial fontanelles prevent neck stiffness, a **diagnostic lumbar puncture** is indicated in suspected sepsis with positive blood cultures, clinical neurological deterioration, or unresponsiveness to therapy. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals pleocytosis exceeding twenty to thirty white cells, protein over one hundred milligrams, and low glucose.
steps.say: Lumbar puncture is essential in proven bacteremia or neurological signs to detect neonatal meningitis.

steps.tx: Empirical first-line antimicrobial therapy for early-onset sepsis combines **intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin**. Ampicillin covers Listeria monocytogenes and Group B Streptococcus, while gentamicin provides synergistic bactericidal activity against enteric Gram-negative bacilli. If hospital-acquired late-onset sepsis is suspected, vancomycin or piperacillin-tazobactam is selected based on local NICU antibiograms.
steps.say: Empirical therapy pairs ampicillin with an aminoglycoside to cover Gram-positive and enteric pathogens.

left.title: First-Line EOS Regimen
points: Ampicillin 100 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours
Gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day once daily
Covers GBS, Listeria, and sensitive E. coli

right.title: Meningitis Dosing Adjustment
points: Double ampicillin dose to 200 to 300 mg/kg/day
Substitute cefotaxime for aminoglycoside
Third-generation cephalosporin crosses blood-brain barrier
